title: Kardajala Kirridarra - Breaking and Entering
transcript:
Producer, vocalist and instrumentalist Beatrice Lewis joined Breaking and Entering in the Triple R studio on 20 July 2017 to discuss Kardajala Kirridarra's debut, the station's Album of the Week. Also a member of Haiku Hands and a solo artist under the name Beatrice, she was introduced as a Red Bull Music Academy alumna and a recent addition to The Operatives roster. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: Welcome back. You used to do a lot of work here as a live-to-air volunteer, and you've been out in the Northern Territory for a while. What originally drew you to volunteer at the station?

Beatrice: Even sitting out there waiting to come in, listening to the music you play, it's the best. It's so inspiring. To me, the music industry is so exciting and diverse, and you guys actually represent that and show that, rather than playing the white boy computer music world, it seems like.

Simon: You worked mainly in production, as a stage assistant and broadcast assistant on our live-to-airs in the Triple R performance space. Are there particular memories that stand out?

Beatrice: Definitely, we were just saying the last one was probably Tune-Yards. That was a standout. I'm a really big fan, and it was cool to see how she sets up and how her gear works. The back end, for gear nerds, that's pretty exciting.

Simon: You do a lot of work in production, but you're also an accomplished live performer. You work as a solo artist, you're part of Haiku Hands and, of course, Kardajala Kirridarra. How do you balance those projects, and do they relate to each other?

Beatrice: Absolutely. It's all the same thing, I guess. It's all women in music, and making really good music that I think hopefully helps make the world a better place.

Lauren: You're also a workshop facilitator in MusicNT's Sista Sounds and Desert Divas programs, and a passionate champion of Indigenous women's music. Can you tell us about the workshops and how you became involved?

Beatrice: That's how I started going up to the desert. I was running youth programs, using music as the tool for teaching and working with people. Then I started working with MusicNT. They run this amazing program called Sista Sounds and a related program, Desert Divas. I worked with them for, I don't know, four or five years. It's going out to remote communities and working with women in those communities, doing production, songwriting and recording, learning what women want. What do you guys want out here? What resources do we have, and how do we share them? Sitting down with all the old ladies out bush, talking story and culture and what their music is. It's a really cool exchange of skills and knowledge and sharing.

Simon: You've described working with artists in the desert as perhaps your most important, life-changing experience. What have you learned during your time there?

Beatrice: Working with Kardajala has been the most recent experience, the last three years. Eleanor, the main vocalist you can hear in that track, is who I started working with. I was about to not go back to the desert, because it had been five years and my own stuff was happening. When you disappear into the desert for three or six months, the music industry doesn't really wait for you. I was like, no more. Then I met Ellie. Just meeting her was incredible. She's a very powerful, important human, and she's telling a really strong story. She's taught me a lot about connection to Country and culture and life. That's the way she exists in the world, how she sits with Country. The way she walks through those boundaries of kardiya world, whitefella world, and culture and more traditional ways of life is really graceful, beautiful and exciting. She's a powerful musician and a powerful person. What she has to say and share with the world is really important, and I'm really honoured to be able to help facilitate that.

Simon: You've identified this project as an opportunity to share Mudburra. In some ways, is this the first time it's been documented in writing, as a traditionally spoken language?

Beatrice: I don't know that personally. I know there's been a language mob going out there quite a bit. Janey Dixon, the elder in the group, is the one who made the bush medicine I just gave you. She's very fluent in Mudburra, so she's been working with linguists out there. It's not traditionally a written language, but even writing it down, it looks pretty weird.

Lauren: You've described it as capable of expressing ideas and thoughts that don't exist in the English language.

Beatrice: It's so nice to learn about culture and knowledge through language. There are words like ngurrmarla, which means love for Country or connection to Country. It's a really beautiful thing you say when you're feeling really good. It's like, ngurrmarla. I don't know how to say it, but I just have my hand on my heart. That's what it feels like, connection to Country and love for Country. Then mandiyala means I feel really sad for Country, but you would also say it if someone is going through a hard time. You'd be like, oh, mandiyala. That's like, I have empathy for you.

Simon: It sounds like a deeply empathetic language, those connections much more powerfully expressed through Mudburra.

Beatrice: Yeah, but Janey Dixon is extremely cheeky and rude, so I also know heaps of rude, naughty words, which is pretty funny.

Lauren: The band name translates as Sandhill Women. I believe it's a strong spirit woman who lives behind the community of Marlinja in the Northern Territory. Can you tell us about the creation story and how it relates to the record?

Beatrice: Kardajala Kirridarra, she's a spirit woman who lives out the back of Marlinja. She became the title of the group because when Eleanor and I first started writing together, we were talking a lot about women's stories and women's empowerment. That's really important for those ladies because, probably the same as kardiya, whitefella music industries, a lot of men's stories get out there, and often the women's stories don't get told as strongly. This album is talking about one woman's journey through life. The Sandhill Woman, Kardajala Kirridarra, represents that feeling of women's stories.

Simon: The record has been three years in development. How did it evolve over that time?

Beatrice: I was working in the desert, and I went to a community called Ali Curung, about two hours south of Tennant Creek in the Northern Territory, almost halfway between Alice Springs and Darwin. I was working with Barkly Regional Council, doing a youth diversionary multimedia music program called Barkly Desert Cultures. We were working with Monkey Marc and Sean Spencer. What was the question?

Simon: It took three years to develop. How did it evolve over time?

Beatrice: I just got so lost thinking about being in Ali Curung. I met Eleanor and got involved with Ellie that way. We wrote the first song you played, 'Abala Barlawa'. I was teaching Ellie how to use Logic, and I don't really know how to use Logic, which is a computer program. So the beats are very simple, and it's all vocals because I only really knew how to record vocals. We wrote that song and worked out it was going to be a really good experience. We started writing music together and working with other women from the community. It's a workshop-based interaction that ended up being really good music, and we all fell in love and started a band, which is awesome.

Simon: You've been talking about connections between language, Country and culture. Country forms part of the sound of the record, because you've recorded on Country. Can you describe those experiences as a producer?

Beatrice: As a producer I take everything I need, which is pretty easy now. There's a lot of really good, high-quality gear you can buy quite cheaply. Sort of cheaply. I would go up to Elliott and Marlinja, where those guys are from. We would set up a studio mainly in the back hall of Marlinja, or in the old abandoned clinic, which had an air conditioner. Sometimes we were recording in summer, which out there is hot. I can't even describe it. I know people in Melbourne are like, it's so hot. I'm like, no, no. We'd have to turn off the air conditioner while we recorded, quickly record, then turn it back on as soon as she was finished. There's lots of Foley sounds from around there. We recorded seed pods and the storm coming in. The skies are really big, and you can often see the edges of the storm coming up on the horizon. There was lots of rain at that time because it's wet season, so we had to stop all the time when it was raining. But I also use my computer, so we had lots of synths and software. It's a nice combination of the two.

Lauren: Haiku Hands recently played Multifuturism, through Multicultural Arts Victoria, a festival challenging outdated notions of the term 'world music'. Throwing Shade, a recent guest, has said that term should be eliminated. You've described Haiku Hands as genreless, socially conscious but not didactic, energetic and entertaining. How do you achieve that?

Beatrice: Listen to the music. I'm really interested in a new space in music that a lot of people are exploring, where it's not about gender or race, it's about really great beats and new, interesting concepts. It's such an exciting time because technology and gear are so accessible. The world feels like it's opening up a little bit. The music industry is totally changing, and all the gatekeepers, no offence out there, but mostly middle-aged white men, it's shifting and changing. I feel excited that all these new directions are happening and people are collaborating. People are getting in touch with us from overseas. We can look at our Spotify plays and see who's playing us, and go to that place. We don't have to wait for someone to invite us. It feels like an empowering time, and I'm really looking forward to what's going to happen next.

Simon: Now the album has been recorded and released, you're able to talk about it and play it live. We understand you've played with Hiatus Kaiyote recently and are working on live visuals. Where are things at with the live presentation?

Beatrice: Things are exciting. We've just finished that body of work, and there's been such a great response. Thank you, Triple R, for calling us Album of the Week. Everyone's response has been amazing, so we're all feeling excited. Our next show is at BIGSOUND, and we're working on that show, thinking about maybe getting some live musicians. The live setup at the moment is the four of us singing, and I do lots of effects on the vocals and beats. We're definitely looking at doing live visuals, because we have incredible footage. The colours are magic, and at every time of the day it's so different. We want to show that. We're working at trying to create a show where you can feel a lot more connected to the desert and to their Country. That's the plan.

Lauren: Congratulations on the record. Can you talk us through 'Two Worlds Collide'?

Beatrice: It's a track we wrote about a young Indigenous woman walking between those two worlds, and what an interesting walk that is, I guess. Not that I don't personally understand, but Ellie and I wrote together about what that's like for her and for a lot of young Indigenous women.
